meanings.note: Friendly, upbeat Brazilian greeting or attention-getter.

examples.trans: Hey there, excuse me, my friend.
Hey there, it is me again.

meanings.note: Used standalone in Brazilian speech as the everyday informal sorry.
With que it is Brazil's most natural everyday way to say I think / do you think.

examples.text: Eu acho que você tá exagerando.

meanings.note: All-purpose connector, relative link, question opener, and comparative word after mais or melhor.

examples.text: Eu acho que ele já foi.
examples.trans: I think that he already left.

meanings.note: Definite article agreeing in gender and number with its noun; also common before given names in casual Brazilian speech.

examples.trans: Look at the young woman over there.

meanings.note: Alone as vocative gente! it means folks/guys; with article a gente it means we/us with third-person singular verbs.

examples.text: Você acha que é melhor que a gente?
examples.trans: Do you think you're better than us?
Oh, folks, the meeting ran late.

meanings.note: Takes present subjunctive entre after querer que (eu quero que você entre).

examples.text: Eu tenho que entrar lá dentro.
examples.trans: I have to go inside there.
I want you to go in too.

meanings.note: Usually contracts with definite articles to no, na, nos, nas.
Traditional Brazilian funeral viewing held before burial.

examples.text: Acho que a gente entrou no velório errado.
examples.trans: I think we walked into the wrong wake.

examples.text: Onde é que tá o velório?

meanings.note: Placed after the noun: no velório errado (into the wrong wake).

examples.text: A gente entrou no velório errado.
examples.trans: We walked into the wrong wake.

meanings.note: Used for identifying a type of meeting or the department a person belongs to. The present forms sou and é are irregular.
Followed by an infinitive for your own wish (quero saber) or que + subjunctive for someone else (quero que você entre).

examples.text: Eu só quero saber o motivo.
examples.trans: I just want to know the reason.

meanings.note: Covers knowing facts or finding out information.

examples.text: Eu só quero saber o motivo.
examples.trans: I just want to know the reason.

meanings.note: Interrogative or relative adverb of place, often reinforced with é que in speech (onde é que tá).

examples.text: Onde é que tá o velório da nossa mãe?
examples.trans: Where is the wake for our mother?

meanings.note: Used here for being present at an event. Vou estar keeps estar in the infinitive after the finite form vou.

examples.trans: I’m not going to be at that meeting.
Are you going to be at that meeting?

meanings.note: Links a meeting with its subject. Do is de + the masculine article o; sou do financeiro identifies membership in the finance department.
First-person plural possessive agreeing in gender and number with the noun.

examples.text: Ela está com a nossa equipe.

meanings.note: Female parent; plural mães.

examples.text: Meu pai e minha mãe me bloquearam.
examples.trans: My dad and my mom blocked me.

examples.text: Vou voltar pra casa da minha mãe.
examples.trans: I am going to go back to my mother's house.

meanings.note: Points to the speaker's location or reinforces demonstratives like isso aqui and esse slide aqui.

examples.text: Ela veio aqui olhar um extintor.
examples.trans: She came here to check an extinguisher.

meanings.note: Between article and noun (a mesma coisa) it means the same.

examples.trans: We work on the same team.

meanings.note: First-person singular possessive agreeing with the thing possessed.

examples.text: O seu tempo vale mais que o meu?
examples.trans: Is your time worth more than mine?

meanings.note: In plural, Meus sentimentos is the standard Brazilian expression for 'My condolences.'

examples.trans: It is right here. My condolences.

meanings.note: Doubled as já, já, it means 'very soon / any minute now'.

examples.trans: Your husband is already doing great.
I have already been in that situation.

meanings.en: can; may; to be able to
meanings.note: Core modal verb followed by an infinitive.

examples.text: O senhor pode ser meu fiador?
examples.trans: Can you be my guarantor, sir?

meanings.note: In Brazilian workplaces and venues, liberar a entrada means to let people in.
Both a physical doorway and permission to enter (liberar a entrada).
Stands without um for another (outro gráfico), or with os for the others (os outros).
Can be used as an adjective or noun for a family member.

examples.text: Não tem um amigo, um familiar?
examples.trans: Don't you have a friend, a family member?

meanings.note: Introduces a contrast. The informal thanks softens the refusal; it does not accept the invitation.

examples.trans: It’s a meeting, but I’m not going.

meanings.note: Third-person feminine singular pronoun; in informal Brazilian speech olha pra ela uses ela after a preposition too.
Has one singular form for both masculine and feminine.

examples.trans: But she looks different, doesn't she?

meanings.note: A negative answer or a negation in a sentence. A final repeated não can reinforce a conversational refusal in Brazil.
Literally 'obliged'; men say obrigado and women say obrigada.

examples.trans: Thank you very much, you hear?

meanings.note: Regular -er verb for grasping meaning or an explanation.

examples.trans: I don't understand any of this.

meanings.note: Versatile core verb; dando falsa esperança means giving false hope.

examples.text: Ele está dando falsa esperança pra nós.
examples.trans: He is giving us false hope.

meanings.note: Informal reduced para. Before a feminine noun, this Brazilian spelling can also represent a contraction including the article a; the exact meeting is clear from context.

examples.trans: Are you going to the meeting?

meanings.note: To bury a body at a funeral.

examples.text: Não dava pra enterrar ela assim.
examples.trans: We could not bury her like that.

examples.text: A família foi enterrar a avó.
examples.trans: The family went to bury their grandmother.

meanings.note: Marks accompaniment or an added ingredient such as sweetener.

examples.text: Ela está com a nossa equipe.

meanings.note: Points to someone or something further away from both speakers.

examples.text: Você tá vendo aquela moça ali?
examples.trans: Do you see that young woman over there?
That chart over there is great.

meanings.note: Often used in the singular in Brazilian salon speech (fazer a sobrancelha, to do one's eyebrows).

examples.text: Ela estava com aquela sobrancelha pra fazer.
examples.trans: She had those eyebrows needing to be done.
She got her eyebrows done yesterday.

meanings.note: Irregular past eu fiz (I made/did); não tem o que fazer means having nothing to do.

examples.text: Ela não tem o que fazer agora.
examples.trans: She has nothing to do now.

examples.text: Esse slide aqui eu fiz ontem.
examples.trans: This slide here I made yesterday.

meanings.note: Ubiquitous spoken contraction of não é used to invite agreement.

examples.text: Isso aqui é um gráfico, né?
examples.trans: This here is a chart, right?

meanings.note: A person being addressed, with third-person verb agreement: você vai, vocês vão. Vai and vão are forms of ir, not forms of the pronoun. Common in Brazil; not a rule that every Brazilian region uses the same address system.

examples.trans: Are you going to the meeting?

meanings.note: Cosmetic hair removal or waxing.
Affectionate family word for mother.
Standard word for a person's face.

examples.trans: On the face it was microblading.

meanings.note: Cosmetic semi-permanent eyebrow or lip shading popular in Brazilian beauty clinics.

examples.trans: On her face it was microblading.
She had microblading done on her eyebrows.

meanings.note: Gerund vendo pairs with estar (tá vendo, do you see), and tem que ver means we have to look into it.

examples.text: Você tá vendo aquela moça ali?
examples.trans: Do you see that young woman over there?
We need to look into that later.

meanings.note: Often reinforced with é que in questions (como é que foi?).

examples.text: Como é que foi a cirurgia?
Como é que tá meu marido?

meanings.note: Facial look or spoken phrase.
Contraction of de + ela, placed after the noun in Brazil to mean her.

examples.trans: She got ahead on her work.

meanings.note: Used in beauty and design for making features stand out.
